title: When a Question Becomes Feedback
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article examines questions as an indirect but powerful feedback delivery method, particularly useful when giving feedback to someone with more status or power, or when a direct evaluation risks defensiveness. It argues that a well-placed question like 'Why did you choose that approach?' functions as feedback because it forces reflection on a decision without requiring the questioner to stake out a position of their own. The piece is careful to name the tool's limitation too: because it's so indirect, the message may not land or prompt real reflection until much later, if at all, so it should be reserved for situations where a direct critique would backfire.
points: Questions work as feedback because they force the recipient into self-generated reflection rather than delivering an external verdict the questioner must defend.
The technique is explicitly recommended for asymmetric-power situations — giving feedback upward to someone with more status — where direct criticism risks backfiring.
The tool's honestly stated limitation is that indirectness can mean the feedback never lands or takes far longer to prompt real reflection than a direct statement would.
quotes: That’s why questions are a powerful tool for delivering feedback indirectly and without the sting of criticism.
When a leader or team member intentionally poses a question to carry feedback, it prompts reflection about a choice.
What makes feedback couched as a question so persuasive is how indirectly tactful it is. The questioner need only raise the issue.
Keep in mind that because of how indirect questions as feedback can be, those on the receiving end may not engage in the reflection necessary for change until much later, if at all.
Questions as feedback should be reserved primarily for those situations where the other person might react negatively to a more direct evaluation or criticism.
